title: Why Your CV Hides What Matters Most
author: William Meller
summary: William Meller introduces the idea of identity capital, the sum of everything a person has done that became part of who they are, as the part of a career that never fits on a CV. He traces the term from Meg Jay's The Defining Decade back to sociologist James Côté, who argued that modern societies dismantled the ready-made scripts into adulthood so that each person must build a path without a map. Meller illustrates with his own story, from a blog started at 13 and freelance articles written at night to pay for his wedding, to giving his first talk in English in Seattle. His key move is a confession: he still treats identity capital like a scheduled savings plan of courses and certifications, when the deposits that mattered most came unplanned. He concludes that identity capital is built sideways, as a side effect of doing uncomfortable things for the right reasons, and asks what ordinary thing done this week will only make sense in ten years.
points: Meller's image: the CV is a car's bodywork, while identity capital is the engine that keeps it running.
Côté coined the concept to explain how people cross into adulthood once the traditional scripts came apart.
A 'fine enough' first talk in a borrowed language changed Meller more than a perfect one could have, because perfection would not have been risked.
Identity capital cannot be accumulated through scheduled deposits like courses; it accrues sideways through uncomfortable choices.
quotes: The simplest definition I can give: it is the sum of everything you have done that became part of who you are. Not what you know. What you became.
Côté’s argument is harder and more interesting: in modern societies, the ready-made paths into adulthood came apart.
Now everyone has to build their own, and identity capital is exactly the resource a person uses to cross that stretch without a map.
And it is funny how “fine enough” changes a person in a way that perfect never would, because perfect you would not have risked.
As if I could open the app and transfer a fixed amount every month into the account of who I want to be. Except the deposits that actually weighed in my life never came scheduled.

Identity capital is not built by chasing it head-on. It gets built sideways, as a side effect of doing the uncomfortable thing for the right reason, and the deposit only shows up on the statement much later.
What are you doing today, in this fairly ordinary week, that will only make sense ten years from now?
